misconceptions.description: The learner treats the limit as another name for evaluation, so a missing or displaced function value is read as a missing or displaced limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a graph with an open circle at one height and a closed point at another over the same input and ask for the limit and the value separately.
misconceptions.name: The limit at a point is the value of the function there

misconceptions.description: The learner treats naming the definition or the theorem as the argument, so the values and conditions that make the claim true are never produced.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which feature of the given function or table makes the stated claim true.
misconceptions.name: Restating a definition counts as a justification

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the infinity symbol as an input value, so end behaviour is computed by substitution and the conditions on degree comparison are skipped.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to divide numerator and denominator by the dominant power and to say what each resulting term approaches.
misconceptions.name: Infinity is a number that can be substituted

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a statement about the long run rate as a statement about the long run amount, so the wrong function is placed inside the limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the units of the limit just written and compare them with the units the question asks about.
misconceptions.name: The end behaviour of a quantity and of its rate are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the conclusion of the Intermediate Value Theorem as producing a unique input, or applies it without checking that the target lies between the endpoint values.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the theorem rules out a second input with the same output and what it would take to find one.
misconceptions.name: An existence theorem locates or counts solutions

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate a limit whose value is infinite from a limit taken as the variable grows without bound, so vertical and horizontal asymptote statements are exchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to point to where the infinity symbol sits in each of two statements and to say what each claims.
misconceptions.name: All limit notation with an infinity symbol means the same thing

misconceptions.description: The learner decides whether a derivative exists from how the curve looks rather than from the one sided behaviour of the difference quotient, so a vertical tangent is read as a slope and a smooth looking point is assumed differentiable.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the slope approached from each side as two separate numbers before the verdict is given.
misconceptions.name: Differentiability is a visual property of the graph

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the two numerator terms as interchangeable and the denominator as carrying no square, so sign and structure errors follow.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to apply the rule to a reciprocal whose derivative the power rule already gives and compare the two results.
misconceptions.name: The quotient rule is symmetric

misconceptions.description: The learner treats differentiation as an operation on the visible outer function, so whatever sits inside is copied across unchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to differentiate the same outer function with a linear inside and with a quadratic inside and to compare the two answers.
misconceptions.name: Differentiation acts only on the outermost shell

misconceptions.description: The learner expects the implicit derivative to come out in x alone, so an expression containing y is read as unfinished and is manipulated until the y disappears.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student for the slope at two different points of the same curve with the same x coordinate.
misconceptions.name: dy/dx is a number rather than an expression in both variables

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the equation on dy/dx as the whole problem, so a value satisfying it is reported without checking that a point with that value lies on the curve.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to verify that the candidate point satisfies the original equation, as a separate step.
misconceptions.name: A tangent condition is a condition on dy/dx alone

misconceptions.description: The learner stores the three formulas as one family and selects among them by resemblance, so the radical and the rational forms are exchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say which of the three derivatives has a square root and why.
misconceptions.name: The inverse trigonometric formulas are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The learner selects a rule by the visual pattern of the expression rather than by the operation applied last, so nested structures are handled in the wrong order.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to state the last operation performed when the expression is evaluated at a number.
misconceptions.name: The differentiation rule follows from the look of the expression

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the second derivative as a separate construction rather than as the derivative of the first derivative, so the same rules are not reapplied.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say what operation turns the first derivative into the second.
misconceptions.name: A higher derivative is a different kind of object

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a contextual question as asking about the modelled quantity regardless of whether the question concerns its amount or its rate of change.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give the value of the function and the value of its derivative at the same input and ask which one answers the question and why.
misconceptions.name: The derivative and the quantity are the same information

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the unit as something added at the end if time allows rather than as part of what the derivative is.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the units of the answer before the computation is done, from the units in the stem alone.
misconceptions.name: Units are an ornament on the answer

misconceptions.description: The learner uses the two words interchangeably, so the sign that records direction is either lost or is reported as part of a speed.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a negative velocity and ask separately for the speed and for the direction of motion.
misconceptions.name: Speed and velocity are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner reads positive acceleration as speeding up, treating the sign of the velocity as irrelevant to the question.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give negative velocity with positive acceleration and ask whether the particle is speeding up.
misconceptions.name: Acceleration alone settles whether speed is increasing

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the tangent line value as the function value rather than as an approximation, so the distinction between the two inputs and the question of error direction do not arise.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask how far the tangent line value is from the function value and which of the two is larger.
misconceptions.name: The tangent line is the function near the point

misconceptions.description: The learner settles whether the tangent line is above or below the curve from the sign of the first derivative rather than from the concavity.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an increasing concave down function and ask for the direction of the tangent line error, then repeat with an increasing concave up function.
misconceptions.name: The direction of the approximation error follows from increase or decrease

misconceptions.description: The learner treats zero over zero and infinity over infinity as values that may be written on the right of an equals sign and manipulated.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say what the symbol on the right of their equals sign names.
misconceptions.name: Indeterminate forms are numbers

misconceptions.description: The learner treats an existence theorem as a rule that applies to any function, so the conditions never enter the written argument.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a function with a jump inside the interval and ask whether the conclusion still holds.
misconceptions.name: Hypotheses are decoration and the conclusion is the theorem

misconceptions.description: The learner believes that writing the name of the theorem completes the argument, so the verified hypothesis and the affirmative conclusion are left out.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which sentence of the response would convince a reader who had never heard of the theorem.
misconceptions.name: Naming a theorem is itself a justification

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the conclusion as naming the input rather than asserting that one exists.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the theorem tells you about where the point is.
misconceptions.name: An existence theorem locates the point it asserts

misconceptions.description: The learner does not check the closed interval and applies the Extreme Value Theorem to open intervals or across discontinuities.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a function on an open interval with no largest value.
misconceptions.name: Continuity may be assumed on any interval

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the derivative being zero as the definition of a turning point, so no sign change is checked.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a function with a zero derivative at an input that is not an extremum.
misconceptions.name: Every critical point is an extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner answers questions about the function by reading features of whatever curve is drawn, even when the drawn curve is a derivative or an integrand.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to label the plotted curve and the function under discussion separately before answering.
misconceptions.name: The plotted curve is the function under discussion

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate the input at which the extremum occurs from the extreme value itself.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for both the input and the value and see which the student had reported.
misconceptions.name: The location of an extremum and its value are the same answer

misconceptions.description: The learner builds the candidate list from the interior critical points and does not regard the endpoints as competitors.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the function value at each end of the interval.
misconceptions.name: The candidates are the critical points only

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a first or second derivative test as a proof that the extremum is the largest or smallest on the whole interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask how the candidate compares with the value at the far end of the interval.
misconceptions.name: A local test settles a global question

misconceptions.description: The learner does not distinguish rising from bending upward, so the sign and the direction of the derivative are used interchangeably.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to sketch a decreasing concave up curve.
misconceptions.name: Concavity and monotonicity are the same property

misconceptions.description: The learner picks a test by habit rather than by what the given representation supports or what the question demands.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which derivative the given object shows and what the question is claiming.
misconceptions.name: The two derivative tests are interchangeable in every setting

misconceptions.description: The learner carries the algebraic domain of the reduced objective into the problem and ignores what the situation permits.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether a negative length would make sense in the situation.
misconceptions.name: The contextual domain is all inputs

misconceptions.description: The learner reports the optimal number and regards the question as answered, with the quantity, the units, and the input left implicit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the number measures and when it is attained.
misconceptions.name: A numerical answer is a complete interpretation

misconceptions.description: The learner differentiates expressions in the second variable without the chain rule, and leaves the derivative symbol unsubstituted.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the derivative of the square of the dependent variable with respect to the independent one.
misconceptions.name: Implicit differentiation may treat the dependent variable as a constant

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a Riemann sum as the value of the definite integral rather than as an approximation whose error has a direction.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the reported sum is larger or smaller than the integral and how the student knows.
misconceptions.name: Riemann sums are exact

misconceptions.description: The learner applies one monotonicity rule to every approximation method, so concavity never enters the reasoning.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an increasing concave down rate and ask for the direction of a trapezoidal estimate and of a left sum separately.
misconceptions.name: Approximation direction follows from increase or decrease alone

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate whether a function rises from whether it bends upward, so the two justifications are exchanged freely.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to sketch a decreasing concave up curve.
misconceptions.name: Concavity and monotonicity are the same property

misconceptions.description: The learner attaches every question about the accumulation function to the visible features of the plotted integrand, so extrema and inflection points are read off the wrong curve.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to label the plotted curve and the accumulation function separately before answering.
misconceptions.name: The plotted curve is the function under discussion

misconceptions.description: The learner uses the zeros of f for every feature of g, so both extrema and inflection points are placed at the same inputs.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask where g has extrema and where g has inflection points on the same graph and compare the two lists.
misconceptions.name: A zero of the integrand is a general turning feature of the accumulation function

misconceptions.description: The learner believes that naming the defining property, such as g changing concavity, answers a request for a reason, without connecting the claim to the supplied representation.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what feature of the given graph makes the stated claim true.
misconceptions.name: Restating a definition counts as a reason

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a first or second derivative test at one input as sufficient for an absolute extremum on a closed interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the endpoints can beat the interior candidate and how that is checked.
misconceptions.name: A relative extremum test settles an absolute extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner reproduces area formulas for triangles, trapezoids, and semicircles without the halving factor.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of a single semicircle of a stated radius.
misconceptions.name: Area formulas are recalled without their fractional factors

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the definite integral as the total area of the region between the graph and the axis, with no sign attached to regions below the axis.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the integral of a rate that is negative on the whole interval.
misconceptions.name: The definite integral measures unsigned area

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the accumulated change as the value of the quantity itself, so the initial condition has no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a rate and two different initial values and ask for the value at the later input in each case.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a rate is the amount of the quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate the integral from the integral divided by the interval length, so the two expressions are described and computed interchangeably.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Show both expressions side by side and ask for the units of each.
misconceptions.name: Average value and accumulated amount are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner applies a difference quotient wherever the word average appears, so an average value request is answered with a slope.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two answers has the units of the function and which has the units of a rate.
misconceptions.name: Average of a function and average rate of change are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner treats u as a shorthand label rather than a change of variable, so limits of integration and differentials carry over unchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the lower limit becomes after the substitution and why.
misconceptions.name: Substitution renames a variable without changing the problem

misconceptions.description: The learner selects substitution from the presence of an inner function alone, without checking that its derivative is present.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write du and point to it inside the integrand.
misconceptions.name: A composite integrand guarantees that substitution applies

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the antiderivative as unique, so the arbitrary constant is decoration rather than part of the answer.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name two different functions with the same given derivative.
misconceptions.name: An antiderivative is a single function

misconceptions.description: The learner treats infinity as an endpoint value rather than as a limiting process, so improper integrals are evaluated by substitution.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the improper integral as a limit before antidifferentiating.
misconceptions.name: Infinity is a number that can be substituted

misconceptions.description: The learner concludes convergence from the integrand approaching zero, so the limit is never examined.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Compare the integrals of one over x and one over x squared on the same infinite interval.
misconceptions.name: Every improper integral of a decaying integrand converges

misconceptions.description: The learner omits the interval or the units because the quantity has been identified.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what would change in the sentence if the interval were different.
misconceptions.name: An interpretation is complete once the quantity is named

misconceptions.description: The learner decides whether an estimate is high or low from the monotonicity of the solution rather than from its concavity.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an increasing concave down solution and ask for the direction of a tangent line estimate.
misconceptions.name: The direction of an approximation follows from increase or decrease

misconceptions.description: The learner antidifferentiates without a constant, so the family collapses and the initial condition has nothing to act on.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the answer would be if the starting value were doubled.
misconceptions.name: The constant of integration is optional

misconceptions.description: The learner reports the number and leaves the quantity, the units, and the direction implicit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the number measures and in what units.
misconceptions.name: A numerical answer is a complete interpretation

misconceptions.description: The learner treats any request for an average as a single procedure and does not separate averaging the function values from averaging its rate of change.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two answers carries the units of the function and which carries the units of a rate.
misconceptions.name: Average value and average rate of change are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner sees the integral as the averaging operation itself, so the division by the length of the interval looks like an optional simplification.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the average value of the constant function two over an interval of length five.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a function is its average

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the integral expression as scratch work that supports the calculator rather than as the object being scored.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write, without the calculator, the expression whose value the calculator reported.
misconceptions.name: A calculator answer stands on its own

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the integral of velocity as the length of the trip, so the sign of the velocity plays no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a velocity that is positive on the first half of an interval and the negative of that on the second half, and ask for both quantities.
misconceptions.name: Distance travelled and net change in position are the same

misconceptions.description: The learner reads an accumulation integral as the quantity itself rather than as the change in it, so the initial value has no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give one rate and two different starting amounts and ask for the value at the later time in each case.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a rate is the amount of the quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner attaches accumulation to every rate in the problem without attending to the direction in which each one moves the quantity.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the stored amount does at a time when the two rates are equal.
misconceptions.name: Two rates acting at once combine by addition

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the first or second derivative test as a complete justification, so the endpoints of the interval are never considered.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a function whose only interior critical point is a relative maximum but whose largest value on the interval is at an endpoint.
misconceptions.name: A local extremum argument settles an absolute extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the sentence as a label for the integral rather than as a statement that must fix the quantity, the interval, and the units.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what would change in the sentence if the limits of the integral were different.
misconceptions.name: An interpretation is complete once the quantity is named

misconceptions.description: The learner chooses limits from the axes of the picture or from the stated domain instead of from where the region actually begins and ends.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which inputs bound the shaded region and why those and not the ends of the axes.
misconceptions.name: Limits of integration are a viewing window rather than a boundary

misconceptions.description: The learner remembers the squared dimension but not the fraction in front of it, so equilateral, triangular, and semicircular sections lose their constants.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of one slice of the named shape with a numerical dimension.
misconceptions.name: Area formulas are recalled without their constant factors

misconceptions.description: The learner reads every definite integral as area under a graph, so a radical integrand is still described as an area and its own form is not examined.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what integrand would give the area under the same graph and compare it with the one displayed.
misconceptions.name: An integral over an interval measures an area

misconceptions.description: The learner remembers that a quotient of the two component rates gives the slope but not which is the numerator, so the reciprocal looks equally acceptable.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the slope should be on a path where the horizontal rate is large and the vertical rate is small.
misconceptions.name: The order of the parametric quotient does not matter

misconceptions.description: The learner integrates the velocity components and takes a magnitude at the end, so a path that doubles back is measured as if it were straight.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for both quantities for a particle that returns to its starting point.
misconceptions.name: Distance travelled in the plane is the size of the net change in position

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the written expression as scratch work supporting the calculator rather than as the object being scored.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the expression the calculator evaluated, without using the calculator.
misconceptions.name: A calculator result stands without its expression

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the accumulation as the position itself rather than as the change in it, so the known position plays no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the same coordinate with the known position moved to a different point.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a velocity component is the coordinate

misconceptions.description: The learner attaches every derivative to motion along the path, so the rate at which the distance from the origin changes is read as a speed and the rate of the angle is left out.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what quantity r measures, and then what the units of the requested rate are.
misconceptions.name: The derivative of r is the speed along the curve

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a derivative test as a complete justification, so the endpoints of the angle interval are never compared.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the value of the coordinate at both ends of the angle interval.
misconceptions.name: A local extremum argument settles a farthest point

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the total of the first few terms as the value of the infinite series, so no limit is taken.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the third and the fourth partial sums and whether both can be the value of the series.
misconceptions.name: A partial sum is the value of the series

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the alternating factor as the whole of the test, so no condition on the sizes of the terms is checked.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an alternating series whose terms do not approach zero and ask whether it converges.
misconceptions.name: Alternating signs alone give convergence

misconceptions.description: The learner collapses the two requirements of the alternating series test into one statement, so only one of them is ever checked or stated.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a sequence that decreases but does not approach zero.
misconceptions.name: Decreasing and tending to zero are a single condition

misconceptions.description: The learner treats an error bound as a formula attached to a partial sum, so neither the alternating series conditions nor the derivative bound is established first.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what has to be true of the series before the alternating series error bound may be used.
misconceptions.name: An error bound can be used without checking its conditions

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the bounding expression as the exact error, so the result is written with an equals sign and no comparison with a tolerance is made.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the approximation is off by exactly that amount or by at most that amount.
misconceptions.name: The bound is the error

misconceptions.description: The learner does not treat the requested degree as binding, so a polynomial is written with an ellipsis or a series is truncated without regard to the request.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask how many terms the requested object has and whether it ends.
misconceptions.name: A Taylor polynomial and a Taylor series are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The learner reports one when the other is requested, so an interval is offered as a radius or a radius is treated as a complete answer about convergence.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the radius and for the interval of the same series in turn.
misconceptions.name: Radius and interval of convergence are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the ratio test result as final, so the endpoints are never examined and the interval is reported open.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the ratio test says at an endpoint where the limit equals one.
misconceptions.name: The open interval from the ratio test is the interval of convergence

misconceptions.description: The learner tests one endpoint and transfers the verdict to the other, or applies the same test at both without checking that its conditions hold at each.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the series becomes at each endpoint and whether the two look alike.
misconceptions.name: The two endpoints behave the same way

misconceptions.description: The learner extends the preservation of the radius to the endpoints, so the interval of the original series is carried over unchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the CED guarantees about a term-by-term derivative and what it does not.
misconceptions.name: A differentiated or integrated series inherits the whole interval

misconceptions.description: The student holds that the sign of acceleration by itself decides whether a particle is speeding up or slowing down, so that negative acceleration is read as slowing down regardless of the direction of travel. The reports name this belief directly as a misconception seen in responses.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a judgement about speed at an instant where velocity and acceleration are both negative, and require the reason to be stated; a student holding this belief answers slowing down.
misconceptions.name: Speed is governed by acceleration alone

misconceptions.description: The student treats the definite integral of velocity and the definite integral of the absolute value of velocity as the same quantity, so displacement is offered where total distance was asked. The 2023 report describes this as an incomplete understanding of the difference between displacement and total distance travelled.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for both the displacement and the total distance over an interval on which the velocity changes sign; a student holding this belief reports the same number twice.
misconceptions.name: The integral of velocity gives total distance

misconceptions.description: The student does not distinguish the variable of differentiation, so implicit differentiation with respect to time is carried out with respect to x, and the several notations for derivative and differential are used interchangeably. The reports describe responses that had difficulty understanding differentiation with respect to a variable other than x.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an implicit relation together with a rate with respect to time and ask for the other rate with respect to time; a student holding this belief produces a derivative with respect to x and stops.
misconceptions.name: Derivatives with respect to x and with respect to t are the same object

misconceptions.description: The student treats the two phrases as synonyms, so a difference quotient is offered for an average value, or the derivative is integrated in place of the function. The 2025 report lists finding average rate of change instead of average value among the two most common misconceptions on that part.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for both the average value of a function and its average rate of change on the same interval; a student holding this belief gives one number for both.
misconceptions.name: Average value and average rate of change are the same quantity
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2023 AB/BC Q1(c), cr-23:4; 2025 AB/BC Q1(A), crabbc-25:3 and crabbc-25:4

misconceptions.description: The student equates the value produced by an error bound formula with the actual error of the approximation, writing the error as equal to the bound or as strictly less than it. The 2025 report states that the error is not equal to the bound and the bound is not strictly less than it, and the 2023 report asks for repeated practice communicating the difference between an error and an error bound.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to state what the bound guarantees about the difference between the approximation and the exact value, using an inequality; a student holding this belief writes an equality.
misconceptions.name: An error bound is the error
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2023 BC Q6(b), cr-23:35 and cr-23:36; 2025 BC Q5(C), crabbc-25:33 and crabbc-25:34

misconceptions.description: The student substitutes the infinity symbol for the variable and computes with the result, so limit notation becomes a formality that can be introduced and then dropped. The 2023 report names arithmetic performed with infinity among the errors in evaluating an improper integral, and the scoring notes are cited as calling this out.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for a convergent improper integral and require every line of the evaluation; a student holding this belief writes a reciprocal of infinity rather than a limit.
misconceptions.name: Infinity is a number available for arithmetic

misconceptions.description: The student recalls a theorem by its conclusion and applies it without establishing the conditions, so continuity is asserted rather than derived from differentiability and the required bracketing values are never shown. The 2025 report states that many students attempted to apply the conclusion of the Intermediate Value Theorem without first explicitly checking the required conditions.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Present a function that fails one hypothesis and ask whether the theorem's conclusion follows; a student holding this belief asserts the conclusion anyway.
misconceptions.name: A theorem's conclusion may be used without its hypotheses
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2023 AB/BC Q1(b), cr-23:3 and cr-23:4; 2025 AB/BC Q3(B), crabbc-25:12 and crabbc-25:14

misconceptions.description: The student appears to treat a sign change of the derivative at one point as sufficient to name an absolute extremum on a closed interval, so endpoints and other critical points are never compared. The reports record the behaviour and describe the arguments as local rather than global; the underlying belief is an inference from that pattern.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for an absolute minimum on a closed interval where the only interior sign change gives a local minimum that is not the global one; a student holding this belief names the interior point.
misconceptions.name: A local sign change establishes a global extremum
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2023 AB/BC Q4(d), cr-23:16; 2025 AB/BC Q1(D), crabbc-25:4; 2025 AB/BC Q4(D), crabbc-25:18

misconceptions.description: The student uses the equals sign to join successive lines of work and to attach a calculator value to a symbolic expression, so unequal objects are declared equal. The reports record the behaviour repeatedly and advise teaching the equals sign as a statement of equality rather than punctuation; the belief itself is an inference.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to say which two quantities each equals sign in their own work claims to be equal; a student holding this belief cannot name them for the linking signs.
misconceptions.name: The equals sign is punctuation between steps

misconceptions.description: The student decides whether a linear approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate without consulting the second derivative, treating the two ideas as independent. The 2022 and 2023 reports record responses that did not use given second derivative information; the belief is inferred from that behaviour.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give the sign of the second derivative on an interval and ask, with reasons, whether a tangent line approximation on that interval overestimates or underestimates; a student holding this belief reasons from the direction of the shift instead.
misconceptions.name: Concavity is unrelated to the accuracy of a tangent line approximation

misconceptions.description: The student uses radius of convergence and interval of convergence interchangeably and does not see the endpoints as a separate question. The 2025 report records responses using imprecise language about the radius of convergence rather than the interval of convergence, and the 2024 report notes that students must supply whichever of the two was requested.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the interval of convergence and then, separately, for the radius; a student holding this belief gives the same object for both and omits the endpoint analysis.
misconceptions.name: The radius and the interval of convergence are the same statement
misconceptions.official_evidence_notes: 2024 BC Q6(c), cr-24:36; 2025 BC Q6(A)(D), crabbc-25:37 and crabbc-25:38

misconceptions.description: The student treats the value of a convergent series as something approached by accumulating terms, so a partial sum is offered where a closed form was asked. The 2022 report records the behaviour and notes that in this course finding the value of a series calls on geometric series content; the belief itself is inferred from that pattern.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the exact value of a geometric series and then for a bound on the error of its third partial sum; a student holding this belief answers both with a decimal from partial sums.
misconceptions.name: A convergent series is evaluated by adding enough terms
